utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We are at the beginning of the Defence case at this moment. Nevertheless, I'd like to deal with a few matters which are still outstanding. I do understand that the Prosecution would like to raise a preliminary matter, but I would not be surprised, Mr. Groome, if it shows up somewhere in the agenda I have before me at this moment. If not, of course you have an opportunity to address whatever. I would like to start with some follow-up from the last week's pre-Defence conference. The Chamber has not yet analysed a newly submitted witness list which is filed by the Defence. I'm saying this because the Chamber was informed that there had been a filing, although it has not been distributed yet. So we expect that this would be the witness list. We have not -- certainly not analysed what was filed, so if there will be any problems, the Chamber will let the Defence know. Second item, Rule 67 disclosure. The Chamber takes note of an agreement which was filed by the parties setting out a plan for further disclosure. There's thus no further need for the Chamber to become involved in this respect at this time, and the Chamber appreciates that the parties were able to find a practical solution and reach an agreement in that respect. The next item is on my agenda Defence preparations. Mr. Lukic, is there any update on any possible further matters which may negatively impact preparations for the Defence case, including technical matters as we have seen them in the recent past several times? Any problems to be reported there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I was just reminded that I should remind Your Honours that there might be some delays in collecting the signatures due to these floodings in Balkans, but that's the only technical issue I can think of right now. For the technical issues inside the Tribunal, we have to check all our passwords and the log-ins if they work, since Mr. Ivetic was not able to check mine or Mr. Stojanovic's. But if there is any problem, we will inform you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as matters stand now, at least no problems, no specific problems are reported. Then of course the Chamber is totally unable to do anything about the flooding and of course we are full of sympathy with those suffering from these extraordinary circumstances in the former Yugoslavia. If there's nothing else, I'll proceed. Yes, the next item on my agenda reads: Rule 92 ter statements and tendering of prior testimony in cross-examination. First, in relation to Rule 92 ter statements taken for other cases, the Chamber notes that these statements sometimes contain references to Rule 65 ter numbers or exhibit numbers of these other cases. The Defence is invited to tender tables of concordance in this respect should it want to rely on such references in its statements, otherwise of course the Chamber will be unable to trace these exhibits. Secondly, at the pre-Defence conference there was a short discussion about the Prosecution's intention to, first, tender parts of a witness's previous testimony in cross-examination and, two, receive clear guide-lines from the Chamber on the procedure to be used when contacting Defence witnesses in order to review such prior testimony. Is there anything you'd like to bring to our attention, Mr. Groome, in respect of these issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And as I said at the pre-Defence conference that we were still -- our thinking on the subject was evolving. So we've now spent several days looking at the issue very carefully and we'd like to make a submission to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So now I would like to thank the Chamber for allowing me to address it in greater detail about our proposal for a way in which we might save some time cross-examining Defence witnesses, by relying on the Prosecution's cross-examination of these witnesses before the Karadzic Chamber. Given the fact that 122 witnesses on Mr. Mladic's list have recently testified in the Karadzic trial, such reliance may result in a significant savings of time. This opportunity for greater efficiency arises because Mr. Mladic and Karadzic were originally charged on the same indictment and the evidence of the common Defence witnesses is often identical. This Chamber should be able to consider the examinations of common witnesses conducted before the Karadzic Chamber. In essence, the Prosecution's proposal and proposed procedure would be as follows: When the Prosecution receives a 92 ter application it will evaluate whether some or all of the cross-examination in the Karadzic case is relevant in this trial. If the Prosecution determines that there would be a significant savings of time in relying on the examinations conducted by our colleagues in the Karadzic case in lieu of asking the same questions before this Chamber we will make an application to admit the prior cross-examination under Rule 92 bis or in the alternative under Rule 89(c) and (f). We will make this motion in our response to the Defence's 92 ter motion and will attach those portions of the cross-examination we seek admission of. The motion would be conditional, that is, it would be conditioned on the Chamber's decision to admit the witness' 92 ter statement. As a general practice, we would not tender the entire cross-examination but only those portions which remain relevant to this case. For example, there may be some cross-examination that relates to specific crimes that are no longer part of the indictment against Mr. Mladic; these would be redacted. The Prosecution would include in its response the amount of time the cross-examination in Karadzic took. This will enable the Chamber to consider how to adjust its guidance regarding the time allotted for cross-examination and ensure that this procedure yields tangible savings of court time. Given the unique relationship between the Mladic and the Karadzic cases, there is no jurisprudence directly on point. There is also no jurisprudence that I am aware of which would prohibit such an approach. There is some jurisprudence from the Appeals Chamber which is informative. In the Aleksovski case the Appeals Chamber dealt with a somewhat analogous situation in their decision of the 16th of February, 1999, entitled: "Decision on the Prosecutor's Appeal on Admissibility of Evidence." In that case, the Trial Chamber admitted the direct and cross-examination of Defence Witness Admiral Domazet from the Blaskic trial pursuant to 89(C) over the Prosecution's objection. The Prosecution appealed the Trial Chamber's decision and it asserted as one of its grounds that the Trial Chamber erred in ruling that the Prosecution's cross-examination in Blaskic satisfied the right to cross-examine the witness before the Aleksovski Chamber. The Appeals Chamber rejected this ground and stated: "It is common ground that the alleged events out of which both men were charged took place in the same area, the Lasva Valley area, and that two proceedings (which arose out of the same indictment) had much in common in both their legal and factual aspects." If the Appeals Chamber affirmed the admission of the cross-examination of a Defence witness from another trial over the Prosecution's objection, surely it can only be proper to do so upon the Prosecution's motion. Your Honour, I have prepared an example of what the package would look like as well as a copy of that decision if that's helpful to the Chamber. I'll ask the usher to assist me to distribute this to the Defence and to the Chamber. Your Honours, I'm ready to answer any questions you may have regarding this. I conclude by saying that this procedure has the potential to save a significant amount of time, alleviate the need for witnesses to repeat testimony they have given to this Tribunal recently. Obviously, a more expeditious trial is something that is in the interests of everyone. And as the Aleksovski Appeals Chamber stated in its decision: "The purpose of the Rules is to promote a fair and expeditious trial and Trial Chambers must have flexibility to achieve this goal." The Prosecution submits that this procedure is fair and will achieve a more expeditious trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Judge Moloto has a question for you. Of course the Defence will have an opportunity to respond but let's first listen to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, where you say the Appeals Chamber ruled that if a Trial Chamber wants to use evidence from another trial, it must do so over the motion of the Prosecution. I'm not quite sure how this resolved the matter that was on appeal because my impression is that the Prosecution was appealing the very ruling by the Trial Chamber. How is one to understand the meaning of that Appeals Chamber ruling? Did they rule in favour of the Prosecution or did they rule against the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It ruled against the Prosecution's position. The Prosecution opposed the admission of the witness's testimony in one Chamber to the Aleksovski Trial Chamber, but the principle that it used in overruling or dismissing the Prosecution's appeal I think is informative here, and that is that the right to cross-examination was satisfied in another case when the case arose from the same indictment and dealt with the same factual and legal questions. And I think that's the situation that we essentially have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even if the Prosecution in the current case would like to add to the cross-examination of the previous case, would they -- would the Prosecution be precluded from doing so?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that we would be precluded. In fact, Your Honour, as the Karadzic cross-examination in some ways focused very much on Mr. Karadzic, we would not be asking that that be before you, but we would be asking to have some supplement to our cross-examination so that all of the issues can be brought before Your Honours. And again to ensure that it really does yield in a savings of time, the Prosecution would provide this Chamber with the time that was used in the Karadzic. So I could imagine the Chamber would say that in a case where the Prosecution introduced the entire cross-examination and that took an hour before the Karadzic Chamber, that the Chamber may say that the guidance which ordinarily gives two and a half hours for cross-examination of 92 ter, the starting point would be an hour and a half or whatever less. Some of the cross-examinations in Karadzic are an hour and a half, two hours, and I expect that there will be some substantial savings, although it is difficult to say with some precision until we get the 92 ter motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it if I could add maybe just one point is that if the Chamber will have noticed in the agreement that we've reached with the Defence, it seems that the general rule will be that the exact Karadzic statement will be now the primary way of adducing a witness's evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although the agreement does foresee the possibility of an additional statement to be taken and to be presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and in those cases the cross-examination I imagine would be limited to that new information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome, before I give an opportunity to Mr. Lukic to respond, I also have one question, and I read from the transcript: You said you will make an application to admit the prior cross-examination under Rule 92 bis or, in the alternative, under Rules 89(c) and (f). Your reference to 92 bis and not to 92 ter, is that -- because Rule 92 bis starts by saying: "A Trial Chamber may dispense with the attendance of a witness in person ..." Which means that the witness would not be there if you would apply Rule 92 bis, whereas under Rule 92 ter the witness still would be present. I understood the -- your reference to 92 bis to be for witnesses who -- for whom statements have been presented by the Defence under Rule 92 ter, so the witness is there to be cross-examined; and therefore, I do not fully understand why you refer to 92 bis rather than to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can explain that. I have considered that 92 ter would also be a vehicle for tendering such evidence; however, we believe it is impractical. It would require the witness to come some extra amount of time to The Hague and listen to the audiotape of their testimony in Karadzic. Such a procedure carries with it the risk that it may disrupt Defence preparations with their witnesses. The proposal we've made also highlights an anomaly in the rules and practices of this Tribunal. When Rule 92 ter is used to adduce prior testimony before this Tribunal, the witness is ordinarily asked to listen to it and make any amendments to his or her answers. When 92 bis is used to adduce the very same evidence, the testimony is considered to be self-authenticating. There is no need to have the witness review and comment. Any dispute about what the witness said can be resolved by listening to the official records of the Tribunal. It is for these reasons that I believe 92 bis is the most appropriate mechanism. Should the Chamber come to the view that 92 bis is not appropriate mechanism, that in the context of unique and particular parity that exists between the witness' evidence between the two cases, that the Chamber should consider admitting the earlier cross-examination pursuant to 89(c) and 89(f). 89(f) allows the Chamber to admit evidence in writing where the interests of justice allow. Clearly, that test is met by the simple fact that it allows Mr. Mladic's trial to proceed more efficiently. And of course 89(c) is a broad grant of authority for the Chamber to admit any evidence it deems to have probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Of course the attestation for Rule 92 bis, there is no specific need -- if an audio does exist, then if it is a verbatim transcription of the witness, so to that extent there seems not to be the major problem whether the transcript reflects what the witness really said because that's, I would say, relatively easy to verify. However, whether the witness still stands by that testimony and whether he would give the same answers, which of course is also part of the attestation, that's of course a matter still to be considered, even under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just add for your consideration, we also imagine that in this proposal that we're making that should the Chamber grant our application under 92 bis, the Defence will know that at the time of our response and will have, I would imagine, an opportunity to re-direct not only on the additional questions we ask but on whatever transcript is brought in in lieu of cross-examination. So I think the witness would have a fair opportunity to clarify any matter that they wish to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we would have to think about this in some detail. Mr. Lukic, any response at this moment on the suggestions made by Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Of course we'll need more time to prepare the full response. On this issue I know that we already filed two motions on this issue objecting, and that's our position at this moment, of course, that we object -- still object this proposition. And what I want to emphasise now is that the Prosecution had even more Karadzic witnesses in their case and we didn't have this tool. The Prosecution is trying to change the rules in their favour after their case. If they wanted to propose this, they were able to propose this at the beginning of their case, not at the beginning of our case. So we deem this to be unfair. They want to have more rights than the Defence, and that would be the outcome if their request is granted. So we strongly oppose to this proposition. We are not willing to give the Prosecution more rights than we had during their case. And we will file our response probably in a week we can do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any problems as far as the Prosecution is concerned to receive an answer in a week from now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. And if the Chamber authorises us, we can do it in the context of a specific application such as the sample that we sent up, the arguments can be equally presented in regards to specific cases rather than in the theoretical absence of such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you have a week to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The matter is important enough to be very carefully considered. However, your short response raises already one question, and perhaps you could assist me in refreshing my memory. Did you ever apply for using the transcript of previous testimony as a vehicle for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we have never applied. It was proposed once by the Prosecution and we did not -- did not go that way. We proceeded in a normal way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- we never applied since it's not in the Rules and it's not in the practice of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll wait for your further response and -- but if I understand you well - and my recollection doesn't serve me in detail on this matter - that the Prosecution where you say they're seeking an advantage we did not have, that they offered at least to you to be in a similar position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only in one case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in one case you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll further consider the matter. Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then a few other matters. On the 12th of May of this year, the Defence informally requested that Mr. Ivetic be granted permission to examine Defence witnesses. The Prosecution indicated that it did not oppose this. On the 13th of May of this year, the Chamber granted this request and informed the parties accordingly through an informal communication. Mr. Ivetic is therefore granted permission to examine Defence witnesses and to make witness-related submissions throughout the Defence case, although only in the presence of lead counsel or co-counsel. A few other matters. The Chamber recalls its fourth decision on Prosecution motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts concerning the rebuttal evidence procedure, a decision which was dated the 2nd of May, 2012, wherein it encouraged the Defence to contribute to the expeditiousness of the trial by clearly stating when it intends to challenge an adjudicated fact during its presentation of evidence. And the Defence is hereby reminded of this encouragement. Among the miscellaneous, the following announcement: The Chamber informs the parties that there will be a non-sitting week right after the summer recess, hence there will be no court between the 18th and the 22nd of August. [Trial Chamber and Legal Officer confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Groome, my suspicion that the matter you announced as a preliminary matter would be dealt with during my agenda items most likely has become reality?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's all the Prosecution had. I thank the Chamber for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other matter to be raised by the Defence? Then is the Defence ready to call its first witness? No protective measures, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours, and the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would then Mr. Sladoje be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sladoje -- at least I presume you are Mr. Sladoje. Before you give evidence, the Rules require --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sladoje. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sladoje, you'll be examined first by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to tell us your name for the record, your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: My name is Mile Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Court whether you provided a written statement to the Mladic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, I provided a written statement and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 65 ter 1D01612 in e-court. Let's look at the first page first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In a minute you will be able to see the first page of the document in front of you on the screen. Mr. Sladoje, do you see a document in front of you and do you see a signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at the last page, page 7 in B/C/S version in the same document. As it is stated in here, your statement has seven pages all together and it contains everything that you stated. And there is a signature below that. Mr. Sladoje, is this your signature as well?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this precisely the statement that you provided to the Mladic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to put the same questions to you today, would you provide identical answers after having made the solemn declaration here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would your answers represent the whole truth about the events that you were questioned about?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, only the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this point I would like to tender Mr. Mile Sladoje's statement into evidence. It is 65 ter 1D01612.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1612 receives number D453, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D453 is admitted. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the following is in keeping with the procedure, I would also like to tender the documents that the Defence team used while taking this witness's statement, and I'm talking about three documents: 65 ter 1D02076, 1D02075, and 1D02074.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2076 receives number D454, Your Honours. Document 1D2075 receives number D455, Your Honours. And document 1D2074 receives number D456, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All three are admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And with your leave, Your Honours, I would like to ask you to allow me to read a summary of this witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. You've explained to the witness the purpose of it. It's not the evidence but it's not just to inform the public on what the examination will be based on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, and the witness is aware of that. Mile Sladoje was born in 1951 in Kalinovik municipality. From 1970 together with his family he lived and worked in Sarajevo. When the war started, he was in his family house in Nedzarici, in Sarajevo. Due to the inter-ethnic tensions and fear, the Serbian population from Nedzarici organised guards around their houses. The first armed conflicts started on the 8th of April, 1992, and the first attack was by Muslim paramilitaries on the Nedzarici neighbourhood. The leader of that attack was Dragan Vikic. That was the neighbourhood where he lived with his family at the time. Witness Mile Sladoje was a member of the Ilidza Brigade which was part of the Sarajevo and Romanija Corps. In the Nedzarici Battalion he performed a number of important duties starting with being the assistant commander of the battalion for morale, religious affairs. He discharged those duties from June 1992 to March 1993, and then from March 1993 to October 1993 he discharged the duties as the commander of that battalion. From October 1993 until the end of the war, he was the assistant commander of the logistics battalion and then also the deputy battalion commander. Throughout the war, the battalion and the Nedzarici settlement were almost completely encircled so that the forces of the BiH army were both in front and behind the positions of his battalion and they were almost in close contact. For that reason, the strategic position of Nedzarici was extremely important because if Nedzarici was taken the 1st Corps of the BiH army would have had a complete link with the 3rd Corps of the BiH army and that would have afforded it a major military supremacy of the Army of Republika Srpska. The positions held by the 1st Corps of BiH army were in civilian areas of Sarajevo. Throughout the war these areas were inhabited by civilians, and the official authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not allow them to leave the city freely. There was no any part of the city which didn't have a military formation or a military facility which was used by the 1st Corps of the BiH army. Throughout the war his battalion had a permanent, a standing, order that fire could only be opened in response to enemy fire and only on observed targets. All military activities were defence activities because his battalion only on one occasion throughout the entire war had an offensive activity against Stup hill in order to repair tactical positions. He never received an order from his superior command nor did he issue an order to subordinate units to attack a civilian facility. That was always reiterated at regular briefings at the brigade command and at briefings at battalion level. He did not have an occasion to see General Mladic personally during the war, nor did he ever receive any direct orders from him. On one occasion General Mladic toured the positions of his battalion, but the witness, Mile Sladoje, was absent from the unit on that particular day. In the battalion command they received intelligence about the facilities which were used by the 1st Corps of the BiH army and they could also ascertain the accuracy of the intelligence by observing from the front line and by observing artillery fire which was opened from some of the positions by the BiH army. The artillery positions of the 1st Corps of the BiH army were very close to the civilian facilities. Sometimes they were in the civilian facilities themselves. There were also situations when they opened fire close to the facilities used by UNPROFOR. When the witness's battalion responded by either opening infantry or artillery fire on those positions, what would happen would be complaints that the Serbian army was targeting civilian positions. In logistical terms and in personnel terms, the battalion was understaffed. Among the officers, they did not have any professionals or career officers. The standing order from the superior command was to be careful about the use of ammunition, i.e., that ammunition could be used only to repel attacks. On the right wing of the positions of his battalion, the BiH army had dug out a tunnel under the airport runway. They received a lot of intelligence about that. The tunnel was used until the end of the war for the members of the 1st Corps to be supplied with the equipment, weapons, and logistics. The witness told us more specifically about the artillery weapons that his battalion had throughout the war. He also told us more specifically about the positions where those weapons were deployed, so one can tell exactly where the mortar shells that were implied in the indictment G6 could have been fired from those weapons and from the positions of his battalion. The witness claims unequivocally that three mortar -- the three mortar shells that allegedly on the 22nd of January, 1994, fell in Alipasino Polje under the control of the BiH army were not fired from the positions of his battalion. And finally, the witness also said that they had two rifles with optical sights; however, he also claims that the allegations from the indictment, indicated as F9, are not correct with regard to the position from which fire was opened. And finally he describes and identifies specific positions of the BiH army from which artillery fire was opened and the shells that fell on Alipasino Polje on 22nd January 1994 could have arrived from there. This was a short summary of the witness's statement, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I correct you, it was not a short summary; it was a very, very long summary. It takes three and a half pages in transcript and that is for a statement in writing of seven pages is a very long summary. The Defence is invited to indeed present short summaries. Before we continue, Mr. Stojanovic, one thing is still a bit puzzling me. You have tendered three associated exhibits. Now, if I look at your motion, you announce that - let me have a look. In the motion you say paragraph 14 there are a total of three associated exhibits to this witness statement as set out in the table that is attached at annex B. And in the conclusion you also seek to have three associated exhibits identified in annex B to be admitted into evidence. However, annex B says: "Associated exhibits which the Defence seeks to tender pursuant to Rule 92 ter ...," and there I find four. The one you've not dealt with is the map of incident F9. Now, was it your intention not to tender that fourth exhibit or did you forget it or -- because your submissions are contradicting?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't mention it at this point deliberately because I was thinking of going through the document with the witness and then tender it. Perhaps in the technical sense if it's more acceptable, then I would take 1D02307 and then we can admit the document if this is preferable before I put any questions on it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's therefore not by mistake. At the same time, it's not tendered pursuant to 92 ter but you still are considering to tender it during the examination of the witness. Then please proceed. We have another seven minutes before we take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With your leave I would like to look at 1D -- 65 ter 02307 in e-court, please. And I would like to put some questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sladoje, we can see some markings in this image and I just wanted to put some questions to you about the markings. The marking showing the line of separation between your battalion and 1st and 2nd Corps of the B&H army, is that a marking that you put in?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The location of the incident marked as F9 in the indictment, the location where a teenage girl was hit by a sniper marked as the crossroad ss of the Adija Mulabegovic Street, is that also a marking that you placed here?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I did not mark the street Adija Mulabegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber who marked that particular spot, the spot of Adija Mulabegovic Street?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: This was used in the Karadzic defence and perhaps somebody from the defence did that, and what I did -- what I marked was the Institute for Blind Children and the line of separation. As for the street, I didn't mark that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to clarify that and that is why I wanted to go item by item. Another reason why I wanted to ask you the following is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, one question first of all: This also seems to be a projected map which is not projected at an angle of 90 degrees but in some way under a different angle which always distorts whatever measurement you would like to make an a map. First of all, could you confirm that this is a not-90-degree-projected map? And second, would you have a better one so that we can use a map which can be used in terms of distances?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I confirm that this is not a 90-degree-angle projection, but since we're not going to be doing any measurements and that is not our objective I believe that there would be no need for this because the questions will actually lead us in a completely different direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll wait for that. At the same time, I would encourage all parties not to use these type of maps because they distort what is usually found on maps. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sladoje, the building or the spot that you marked, the Institute for the Blind, is it on the actual line of separation between your battalion B&H army units?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, it is exactly on the line of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, how big is this building? How many floors does it have?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I think that it's a three-floor building, three-storey building. I'm not sure but I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did your unit at any point in time during the war - and I kindly ask you to focus on 1994 in particular - in its combat disposition ever had crews, battalion members, who had rifles with optical sights in this particular building?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: We just had fortifications and classic trenches in this building or facility. We never had such rifles in this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the building behind this Institute for the Blind building is the Oslobodjenje publishing and newspaper company?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And was that then at that time in the defence sector of the B&H army?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, and in particular during 1994, did you -- were you exposed to fire from these positions?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: A part of the Oslobodjenje building was already demolished so there was no shooting from there, but there were other buildings nearby that were 10- or 15-storey buildings from where there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to finish with this document. I would kindly ask you to tell us about this building in red which is a bit lower in relation to the Institute for the Blind. I don't know if you're able to see it. Do you know -- and this building is also literally on the line of separation, do you know what this building is?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: This is also a facility for the blind for adults who underwent rehabilitation there. Before the war it was a clothing factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And was that building also called Institute for the Blind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm lost what building you are referring to at this moment. You said -- you asked about the Institute for the Blind. You have not invited the witness yet to point at that in the map, and then you say a little bit further down there is a building in red. I have no idea what you are talking about and I'm surprised that the witness does. But could we invite the witness to mark what he's talking about, what the Institute for the Blind is, and mark what you refer to as another red building. Would you guide the witness to do so so the Chamber knows --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were talking about the rehabilitation facility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, could we take out any marking which you made on your own initiative. You are supposed to not mark anything unless instructed to do that. So we have a clean map now again. Listen carefully to Mr. Stojanovic and he'll invite you if any need to make markings. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to ask you to place a circle around the Institute for the Blind facility for adults, where adults underwent rehabilitation and where they worked. Could you please mark that on the map.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you the following. At any point during the war did you have positions there from your battalion who used rifles with optical sights?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: We had normal infantry weaponry. We never had snipers or such rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to finish with this question. Since you come from that area, could you see the street Adija Mulabegovic from this particular spot? Did you have a clear line of vision from that spot?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: It was perhaps possible to see the very beginning of Adija Mulabegovic, former Djure Jaksica Street, but then later on you couldn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to mark the circle that you drew with the letters Z S, Zavod za Slijepe, Institute for the Blind.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to tender document 65 ter 1D02077.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, what you've marked, Witness, is that the Institute for the Blind of adults?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were two facilities for the blind within a distance of 100 metres apart. The first one was the Institute for the Blind Children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then -- if you just answer my question, the answer therefore is most likely: Yes, what you marked is the Institute for the Blind who are adults. Could you also mark the Institute which is the Institute for the Blind Children. Could you do that on this map. Or was that what you marked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I marked just now and marked with the letters ZS is the Institute for Blind Adults. Now I'm going to mark the Institute for Blind Children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is the building which was already marked in red before and that is the upper of the two markings where it reads: "Zavod za Slijepe decu" or something like that, but where there is text added. Any objection against admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, with the limitation that Mr. Stojanovic has put on it, that distances -- it's not to be used for distances, only for locations, given the projection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, in the transcript I find the number 1D02077. This is how it was interpreted. Perhaps you can check if that is really the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have just been warned the number is incorrect. So it's the 65 ter number 1D02307.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now in a version as marked by the witness. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours document 1D2307 as marked by the witness receives number D457, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D457 is admitted. We take a break. We will first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break of half an hour, therefore we'll resume at ten minutes past 11.00. Mr. Stojanovic, until now you've used close to half an hour and Your estimate was 45 minutes. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could I just ask that we pull up in e-court the document which is now marked D454.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I will ask you, Witness, to tell me. These locations that are marked with these little circles were the positions from which you say you were fired at. I'd like to ask you about the position which is below the facility marked as Geodetski Zavod, the surveying institute. What was there before 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I believe it was a police station before the war and I believe it is still a police station, it's still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, the information you had as one of the warring parties, was this building used for military purposes still in 1994 and were you fired at from there?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: It was used throughout the war as a military installation. We suffered from artillery fire from that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Right there is Gete street and that is connected with the scheduled incident G6 that you speak about in your statement. Now, from the position you marked, did you have any optical visibility? Did you have a line of vision from Gete Street towards Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No, we did not, but Alipasino Polje was ahead of us and in the last -- this is the last stage, a settlement called Alipasino Polje C.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll be finishing with this document. You mentioned regarding the incident marked in the indictment as G6 that in your view those three mortar shells could have arrived from the west, namely, from the Sigma building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue. Mr. Stojanovic, Gete Street, where are we supposed to find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's just before this circle that the witness discussed, the square of independence, Trg Nezavisnosti and Gete Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see something which can be spelled as G-e-t-e-o-v-a. Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I found it. And Now let's have a look at your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I'll repeat the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question was: Did you have a line of vision from Gete Street towards Alipasino Polje? And could you please then be very clear on what you refer to exactly as Alipasino Polje, which seems to be an area, and for a line of vision or a line of sight you need two points to see whether you can see from one point the other point. I'm a bit lost. And Mr. Groome is on his feet. Even to confuse me more, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm lost as well. Could I ask since there are numerous circles on this, could Mr. Stojanovic please have him mark the circle that means -- that indicates the police station. It's unclear to me what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see -- what I understood, Mr. Stojanovic, is that you referred to the circle which is just below the oval with the text "Geodetski Zavod." Just below that there is a circle. Just above where it reads "Prvomajska" that's what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also -- but let me just re-read what the witness said. One second, please. Well, where the witness said: We did not -- we did not, but Alipasino Polje was ahead of it. And in the last stage a settlement called Alipasino Polje C, that's an answer which is for me at least incomprehensible as to how to understand this. So could you please put clear questions to the witness and seek to clarify whatever answer he gives if it is not immediately comprehensible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think we had a problem in interpretation, but I believe the witness understood me. I'll ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, from the positions that you marked on this photograph and the positions that you militarily held in 1994, did you have a direct line of vision to the area of Gete Street?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: From the line of separation and the positions we held, we had no line of vision because there were tall buildings ahead of us and we couldn't see through to there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I have a problem when you say from the positions that you marked on this photograph. Now, there are lots of markings on this photograph. I don't know from which position the witness did not have a line of vision. I am also lost now. The question was: "From the positions that you marked on this photograph and the positions that you militarily held in 1994, did you have a direct line of vision to the area of Gete Street?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. To clear this up completely, the question was, just as we see this marking in the bottom left corner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which markings? Let the witness show us the marking --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the line of separation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- where from -- the position from where he was. Can you show us which marking you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave then we can ask the witness to mark the position that he held together with his battalion in 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this line which makes an angle of approximately 90 degrees and which breaks at the Institute for Blind Children, what does it represent?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Those were the positions we held, the positions we controlled. It happened to be this shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what is the feature that you encircled, what is this street?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: This is Gete Street and the building behind is the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll finish with this question. You mentioned in your statement the Sigma building. Where was it relative to Gete Street?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: It was to the west of Gete Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1994, were you targeted by artillery fire from the ABH positions near the Sigma building?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, from the Sigma building and another feature which was actually the agricultural complex of Butmir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you want the Chamber to understand where the Sigma building is -- I mean, "west" gives us 40.000 kilometres from the position you indicated. So therefore, try to take us by the hand and tell us where the Sigma building is or ask -- invite the witness to tell us where the Sigma building is, rather than leaving us with 40.000 kilometres to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This agricultural complex and the Sigma building, how far were they -- how far are they, as the crow flies, from Gete Street?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: The distance to the Sigma building and the agricultural complex is approximately 2 and a half to 3 kilometres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From what type of mortar were you fired at from that direction?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: The 82-millimetre and 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for answering my questions. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would appreciate your instructions. This document has been admitted as D454, and now the witness added some markings. Do we need to give a new number to the document now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has this been admitted as D454? Oh, without the marking. Yes, then we should -- if you please would tender it now as a map marked by the witness. Madam Registrar, the number would be? But, Mr. Groome, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D454 as marked by the witness receives number D458, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With your leave, if I could consult with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. And perhaps we'll wait for a second before you start your cross-examination, Mr. Groome, so that Mr. Stojanovic has an opportunity to consult. Meanwhile, I already can tell you, Mr. Sladoje, that you'll be cross-examined soon by Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before I ask you other questions, I just want to clarify what we see now in D458 in front of us. The blue circle that you drew in Alipasino Polje, that's simply a mark to locate a particular street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So where all the other circles on this map that you prepared for Karadzic case, this particular -- those circles refer to places you believed to be military targets. This particular blue circle does not indicate the existence of any military target there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: You're right. All these elliptoid circle markings used to be agricultural buildings converted into military facilities during the war and this Gete Street was populated by civilians. There was only a police station nearby, so we did not identify it as a military installation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I may want to show this, your diagram, to another witness. So could I trouble you to please perhaps with the red pen just mark the English letters or -- for the abbreviation police station, the letters P and S next to the circle where you say the police station was.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And maybe put the letter P and the letter S next to that.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that that be now admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, with another marking, a marking in red added by the witness to the previous exhibit. Madam Registrar, it would now receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D458 as marked by the witness receives number P6507, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you some general questions about your command. Am I correct in saying that the barracks of your battalion was in Nedzarici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: It was in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the headquarters of your battalion was in the barracks at Nedzarici; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to a location that you've referred to as the Institute for Blind Children. Am I correct that that location is approximately 300 to 350 metres from your barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Thereabouts. You're probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in your statement that's now D453 in evidence at paragraph 7 you talk about the faculty of theology. Am I correct that the faculty of theology was approximately 150 to 200 metres from the barracks compound?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at the end of 1993 did the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade, were they combined to form a single battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the headquarters of this combined battalion was located on Kasindolska Street; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the area of responsibility of this combined battalion also included Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did it include Aerodromska Naselje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did it include Kasindol?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sladoje, can you please estimate the total number of mortars that were fired by your battalion over the course of the three years of the conflict? I'm just looking for a general approximation.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer your question. I don't know, not even approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that -- is that because so many mortars were fired that you have difficulty approximating a general number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. That's not the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what's the objection, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way the question is structured. The previous question was whether he could provide a general approximation and the witness said that he could not even give an approximate -- a general approximation. And then the question was whether it was due to the fact that so many mortars were fired. The witness, however, didn't say either "many" or "few." He could not give any kind of information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what is suggested in the question and that's what makes it a leading question and that is permitted in cross-examination, Mr. Stojanovic. So therefore -- Mr. Mladic apparently wants to consult with you, but meanwhile Mr. Groome may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to tell us, is it in the hundreds? Is it in the thousands?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I told you that I could not give you even an approximate number. I didn't count mortars because it was not just us but also the enemy who fired mortars. So really, one couldn't say who fired what and how many. I was not in charge of that. That's why I don't know. If I could give you an approximation, I could, I could tell you 50 or 50.000, but whatever I gave you at this point would not be relevant information because I don't have any relevant information to impart.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So would it stand to reason if I asked you about how many mortars were fired on a particular day, let's say the 8th of August, 1992, would it be correct that you would be unable to assist me with the number of mortars fired on that day as well?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, but I don't know which incident you have in mind. I don't know what may have occurred on the 8th of August. It's really not something that I could objectively know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in March 1993 you succeeded Radivoje Grkovic as commander of the Nedzarici area; correct? I see you nodded your head, but we need to hear your answer for it to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No, no. I seem to have "1992." Is that what you said? But that was in March 1993, so I don't know whether I misheard or whether you were misinterpreted or whether you misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, now the record is clear that it was in March 1993; correct? Were you replaced by Svetozar Guzina who took the post of battalion commander when the three battalions were combined into one?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to call before you an exhibit that you marked in the Karadzic case and that is 65 ter 30629, and it's a variation of the map that Mr. Stojanovic has been working with today. Now, in the bottom right-hand corner am I correct in saying that that bears your signature and the date of the 27th of November, 2012?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I ask that we focus on the left-hand side of the exhibit. In the lower left-hand corner of this exhibit we see a green line. Am I correct in stating that this green line marks the perimeter of the area of responsibility of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that was drawn by you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that the area above the green line and onto the red line was within your responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the newly established battalion is what I marked in red and then something was added in green, and the rest was the enemy's side outside of the lines that are -- have been drawn here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Correct. So that the space above the green but below the red, that's area under your control?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the red rectangle on the left-hand side of the page, it approximates the location of the barracks where the Nedzarici Battalion headquarters were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Well, it is marked here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I just want to confirm these markings. So that is where the barracks is located?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And we can see the letters KP and the fork in the road just beyond the airport. Was this the location sometimes of a check-point that was within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: That was not a classical check-point. We did not have any troops there. However, in view of the fact that the Muslim side was in Stupska Street and that they -- that UNPROFOR soldiers also passed along that way, there was some containers there, there was some sandbags there, and the UNPROFOR unit was known as Sierra 4. This is marked as a check-point because in the Karadzic case Mrs. Edgerton asked me whether there was a check-point there. That's why I actually marked this position at K5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 27 of D453 you describe an event in which flak jackets were confiscated from French forces. Am I correct that where you've marked KP is the location where this happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: You are right. You see, we had information --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll ask you about that --

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: -- that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- in a few minutes. I just want to make sure we orient ourselves to the locations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could you also seek clarification for the reference to K5 which I have not found yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can Your Honour direct me to a line number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, page 41, the line 5, last word -- 4: "That's why I actually marked this position at K5." Or did you intend to refer to KP, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The transcript recorded you as saying "K5," but were you referring to "KP," what's marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Not "K5" but "KP."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just above that KP mark we see a small red circle. Am I correct in saying that your battalion had between four and five mortars located here?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Very close by. Some hundred metres away from the school of theology in the residential area itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you to look for the location of the theological seminary and if you can find it, can you please circle the location and place the letters TS next to it. Perhaps if we use the colour red since I think blue has been used with the witness with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No. The theological seminary is marked in red.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are invited to mark where the theological faculty is which you said was at a distance of some hundred metres from where the mortars were. So could you indicate where the premises of the theological faculty is and could you please mark that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you've marked that with the letters TF. Now, were mortars located at this location throughout the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender 65 ter 30629 with the additional markings made by Mr. Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- no objections, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 65 ter 30629 as marked by the witness receives number P6508, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And yes, what I should say is that "additionally marked by the witness," because the original one was already a document marked by the witness, so additionally marked and is admitted into evidence as P6508.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to return to the incident involving the flak jackets. In paragraph 27 of your statement where you talk about confiscating those flak jackets belonging to French forces, you say: "Towards the end of 1994 we stopped a convoy of the French Battalion because we had information that they were transporting weapons and equipment for the Muslim forces." And then you go on to describe stopping the convoy and confiscating the jackets. Now, my question is the following: Where you stopped and confiscated the jackets, that was just outside the airport; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Some 200 metres away from the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the information that you had about the French transporting weapons, that was from your brigade command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Not from the commander but from our intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You did not find any weapons, did you, just flak jackets?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Only flak jackets, 126 pieces all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my question to you is whether the information you received about what the French had, was that incorrect? Or have you perhaps made a mistake in your recollection about the information you were provided?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: We received information about weapons and flak jackets were being transported. The French Battalion was deployed at the airport. They didn't have any units in the town, so it would have been illogical if they transported things for somebody else and there was no need for them to be supplied by anybody else. That's why we confiscated everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just to make the point that the information you received was incorrect with respect to weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sladoje, I want to show you a series of photographs to help the Chamber understand your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 30633. It's a panoramic photo from the theological faculty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You'll see that photograph in a few minutes or a few seconds. Can I ask you to look at it, orient yourself. And then my question is: Does it fairly depict the area around the theological seminary?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: The school of theology is being renovated. This was not taken during the war. And the houses that you see in Nedzarici is where we were and where we lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So this does fairly depict the area surrounding the theological faculty?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I draw your attention to the -- where the truck that we see in the right-hand side of the photograph, is this where the mortars were located, the four to five mortars that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: They were located there at the beginning of the war and later on they were next to the green meadow, that's where they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to put the letter M to show us -- maybe a circle where the mortars were located and the letter M?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, at the beginning of the war or where they were located later?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to put M1 for the beginning of the war and M2 for this later period.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And then -- okay, I see both. Now, can we see the development of Alipasino Polje in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: From the positions where the mortars were deployed you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, no. From this photograph, can you mark the towers, can you see the apartment towers of that apartment complex?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to put the letters AP just above them to indicate where they are.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, can you give us the approximate date when the mortars were moved from this first position to this second position.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I believe that that was in late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I tender at this stage 65 ter 30633 with these markings made by Mr. Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30633 receives number P6509, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Again, if there's no clear objection, I will usually ask Madam Registrar to assign a number even without explicitly having asked for whether there are any objections. I expect the parties to act on their own initiative under those circumstances. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now take a look at 65 ter 30630.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sladoje, I'm going to show you some close-ups of this panoramic photo and these are ones that you made markings on in the Karadzic case. I am simply going to ask you to confirm what your markings mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So we could perhaps zoom in on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in 30630 we can see the letter M circled in the centre of that photograph? Am I correct that this represents the area Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And we can see a VP circle to the left. Am I correct that this represents Vojnicko Polje; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Vojnicko Polje, military field.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask now that we see 65 ter 30631.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is another close-up of this photo. And my question to you after you have had a chance to look at this, am I correct that when you marked this photo D1, you did that to indicate the location of the residential apartment complex known as Dobrinja 1?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You also marked D5 to indicate the location of Dobrinja 5; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And both of these were large apartment complexes where many people lived; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage I would tender 65 ter numbers 30630 and 30631.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want them to be one exhibit or two exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think perhaps two exhibits, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That perhaps makes it easier. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30630 receives number P6510 and document 30631 receives number P6511, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to now ask you about different portions of your statement. Your statement has been admitted into evidence and the Chamber has read it. There is no need to repeat what's in the statement, but perhaps just focus on the additional information that I am requesting. Okay. Now, in paragraph 3 of your statement you said that in 1991 a Muslim colleague asked you to sell him ammunition; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No, just the opposite, to buy ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. He wanted to buy ammunition from you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No, he wanted to sell ammunition to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Let's just take a look at that. Your -- I'll read you how your statement has been recorded, and if we need to correct it or if you need to correct it, please let us know. Paragraph 3 reads: "In the course of 1991 one of my Muslim colleagues asked me if I was interested in selling ammunition ..." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: That may be so written; however, you need to read the entire statement. If he said if I was willing to sell ammunition and then I go on to say that already in 1991 Muslims had been prepared for war. So I had no reason to sell ammunition. He actually offered me to buy ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He wanted to buy ammunition from you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No, no, he wanted to sell ammunition to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I think that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, could I ask the court officer to bring up P3 in e-court, page 37 to our screens. Your Honours, this is page 32 in the Sarajevo map book.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to your evidence regarding a shelling which occurred on the 22nd of January, 1994, in which six children were killed and five people were wounded. You provide evidence about this event at paragraph 30 of your statement. I want to read you an excerpt of that paragraph and then ask you a question. "In connection with the allegations that the shell was fired from the west, I should point out that the shell was fired from behind the lines from the western side, that is, from the Sigma building, i.e., from positions controlled by BH army forces." Do you still maintain that the shell that killed those children was fired from the Sigma building in the BH army position? A simple yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you accept that according to your evidence that shelling an area where children were playing was a crime?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Absolutely.
