utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you acknowledge that what happened was a crime. Your evidence is that the shell that fell on the children or the shells that fell that day was from the BH army. Do I understand your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I direct your attention to the map in front of you. I want you to simply make a note, a mental note of where G6 and that green dot next to it is. That's the precise location of where this -- these shells fell. When you've made a note of that, let me know and I'm going to change the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could you assist me in the green dot, that is just under the word "Polje"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- to the left of G6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I could say to the south-west of G6, close to it. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if we could call up I believe it's P6507.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is your map of the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we could focus in on the "Alipasino Polje."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that during the course of the war your evidence now at this point is that you never knew there to be any military targets or personnel at the location that we've just seen in the previous map, the place where the shells landed on the 22nd of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I stand by the fact that there was no building there because I think you couldn't really put anything there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were the commander at this time. Would you agree that there was no military objective to be achieved on this day by shelling the location of G6 where that green dot was?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Could you please tell me the date. I'm not quite sure which date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: 22nd of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Well, it's not that important. I wasn't the commander at the time, but I was in the battalion. You insist that it was not a military facility and I understand you, but I can also respond by saying that we did not have a line of sight there. We couldn't have known that children were playing there or anything like that. We couldn't see it. We never did anything like that in any cases during the war. During combat some incidents could happen, but I think that there was no case when anything like that was done deliberately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, on the day that I'm concerned with, you know of no military object that was actively there, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: That is correct, there was no military object there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, there was a series of three mortars that landed in this group of apartment buildings around the same time. Would you agree that such an event would likely instill feelings of terror among the people living there?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Instilling terror is a very serious term. In combat there is no terrorising because there was a police station nearby, the Geodetski Institute was there. So when responding to fire the civilians here --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about this specific event on this very specific day. What I'm asking you is whether you agree it would be likely that the children playing there, their parents in the apartments, that they would have experienced this event - three mortars landing where the children played - they would have experienced that as terror?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness is being asked to speculate about how other people and children could have understood shelling in war time and this is something that the witness cannot know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree with Mr. Groome that it would be very scary for children playing there where three mortars fell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's scary for any normal person, but there are other indications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Indications of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are indications by the Prosecutor that this is terrorism, there is insistence upon it, and I am absolutely asserting that that is not the case and that's why I say that there are other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I invite the English interpreter to move a little bit closer to the microphone because it's quite ununderstandable sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now with respect to your conclusion that the mortar was fired from the Sigma building, am I correct that you did not yourself personally see the mortar when it was fired?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No, I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You did not go to where the mortar landed and conduct any type of investigation, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I couldn't -- Prosecutor, sir, I couldn't even go and see the place because it was under Muslim control. It was far away from me, so I couldn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I know it was an obvious question, but I want to establish that you did not participate in any investigation of any kind related to this event; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter 30634 on our screens. This is the witness's 92 ter statement for the Karadzic case. It was signed by him on the 25th of November, 2012. And could I ask that we please go to e-court page 5 where the witness provides evidence of this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you speak about this event in paragraph 26 of your Karadzic statement which is quite similar but with respect to this particular event you have left out a sentence. The sentence you left out was: "It has been explained to me that on 12 July 1993 an incident occurred in Spasenije Cane Babovic Street and that according to the findings of the Muslim police the area from which the projectile was launched was Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I could repeat the question. I read from the wrong paragraph. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's paragraph 27 that I want to direct your attention to. And the sentence -- just one second, please. The sentence that has been left out is: "It has been explained to me that on 22 January 1994 an incident occurred in Klare Cetkin Street and the Cetinjska Street and that according to the findings of the Muslim police the projectile was allegedly fired from the Nedzarici sector/the Home for Blind Children." Do you acknowledge that that sentence has been left out? Is this my statement in the Karadzic or in the present case?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The statement before you now is from the Karadzic case. That sentence does not appear in D453. Do you acknowledge that or would you like me to call up D453?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: This is what I said and I stand by it because that's how it was. That's how it was in the preparations. I don't know how it came about that this sentence was left out of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we're at the time for the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are. And the last break was longer than we usually have. I have to get back to the daily routine again. So now we take a break of 20 minutes. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think it might be fairer to the witness if I'm going to be comparing to the two statements that he have access to both at the same time. So I have a copy of his -- hard copy of the Mladic statement, I've shown it to Mr. Lukic and he has no objection that the witness have it before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ask the assistance of the usher once he has returned with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist Mr. Groome giving a document to the witness. There's no need to show it to the Defence first. Yes. Witness, you'll be provided with a hard copy of your Karadzic statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Karadzic is on the screen and Mladic is in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, Mladic is in hard copy. So that you're able to read them in comparison. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Sladoje, I just want to confirm that you understand the hard copy, the typed version in front of you is your statement that was tendered in this case, and the one that we have on the screen is the one that was tendered in the Karadzic case. Okay? So if I can pick up where we left off, so if you look on the screen paragraph 27, this is your statement in the Karadzic case, the sentence, first sentence: "It has been explained to me ..." And it continues on. That sentence has been dropped in the statement for this case. So my first question regarding this is: Who is it that explained details about this event to you? Who is the person who did that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No one explained it to me. There's nothing that needed to be explained to me. I explained it and it was in this statement but it's not in this statement here. I don't know how that happened, but this is the statement and these are the facts that you and I can talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I just -- you just told Mr. Groome that you were not there. So whether an incident occurred in those streets you couldn't know it from your own observation. Therefore, the question is: Who told you that this happened there? Or how did you otherwise learn about this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, which incident are we talking about, 27?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking about what is in your statement incident G6, which is found in the statement in this case in paragraph 30 of your statement and which you see on your screen in paragraph 27 of the Karadzic statement. Explosion, children playing, Klare Cetkin Street, Cetinjska Street. That's what we are talking about. 22nd of January 1994. Could you tell us how you learned about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found out about it from the media after a few days because the TV reported about it and this happened later during preparations for the Defence of Dr. Karadzic. This was presented and based on that I provided the statement as you see it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so it's from the media that you learned about it or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you also learn from the media that it was fired from the Sigma building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because this is something that was reported by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I leave it further in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you've just said in reference to the Karadzic statement: "This was presented and based on that I provided the statement ..." Are you saying that the statement was presented to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No, the statement was not presented. The incident when we were working on the basis of the indictment, when we were working down that list, I said what I said and what is presented here in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So when -- again when it says "it has been explained to me," was it explained to you by a member of the Karadzic team or by Mr. Karadzic himself? Was that who explained the information to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I don't know this term "explained." Perhaps I misused it at a certain point, but nobody explained anything to me. There was no need for anyone to explain anything to me. I know what happened on the basis of fact. That's -- the most important thing here is that it was not possible to fire the shell from the Institute of the Blind because there were no mortars there throughout the whole war and that is the gist of this whole matter here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it have been possible, just possible, to have fired at this location from the locations you've marked, M1 and M2 on the picture from -- taken at the theological faculty?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: It's possible but it was not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there's another notable admission from your version of the evidence in the Karadzic case and here. Now, if I could ask you to look at paragraph 30 on the copy that's on your desk and paragraph 27 on the screen. The following sentence that you have in the Karadzic statement has been deleted in this case. "I also affirm that no one from our command had ordered the shelling of the place where the incident allegedly occurred ..." My simple question at this stage is: You agree with me that that sentence is not in your Mladic statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: It's true it's not in the Mladic statement because that statement was given one year later and we were not copying anything, but the gist is that it relates to same incident, only it was added --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- so that sentence, you agree, was removed. Now my question is: Was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- that's not what the witness said. The witness said it's not in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it was removed or not is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That sentence is no longer there. Is it true that that sentence was deleted because you can no longer affirm under oath that your command did not order the shelling that killed the six children? Is that why that sentence is no longer there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. In paragraph 30 of the witness's statement in the Mladic case, the beginning reads: "There is no order to open fire ..." It's exactly the same in content as the sentence that was deleted because otherwise it would be a repetition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not exactly the same, but Mr. Groome is invited to rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, let me just point out to paragraph 18 of the statement this witness gave to us in the Mladic case where he said the same thing explicitly. So I did not feel the need to repeat the same thing three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to explain how you drafted this statement. That is argument which comes later. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Sladoje, you've heard Mr. Stojanovic's explanation as to why the sentence is no longer there. Is that -- do you agree with that explanation?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, I can, and it says here too: "There was no order to open fire." There was no mortar at the location of the Institute for Blind Children. And I confirm what you just said. It's explicitly said here that there was no order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when I look at the two statements it's also noticed that there are some assertions in the Mladic statement that were not in the Karadzic statement, and I want to deal with them now. And again at paragraph 30 in your Mladic statement you write: "I should point out that the shell was fired from behind the lines from the western side, that is, from the Sigma building, i.e., from positions controlled by the BH army forces." Now, my first very simple question is: Do you acknowledge that that sentence does not exist in your Karadzic statement, that that's a new assertion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So now in the context of this case you have signed a statement more than 20 years after the event in which you assert for the first time that BH forces fired the shell on the 22nd of January, 1994, from the Sigma building, an area under their control? This is the first time that you are giving that as evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: In the Karadzic case I asserted - and that's the point - that the shell was not fired from the Institute for Blind Children. That was the point. And perhaps this is put too strongly here when it says I emphasise that the shell was fired from the west from the position of the Sigma building. I cannot be sure. It's my assumption because it came from the west. I know that they had mortars in that location and in the location of the Butmir agricultural complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that was -- that's the point I want to get at. You accept that that's an assumption that you've included in this statement that was not in your Karadzic statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, when I first started asking you questions, I was asking you about the approximate number of total mortars and I asked you about whether you recalled what might have happened on the 8th of August and you were unable to do so. Is it fair to say that you have no specific independent recollection of what happened on the 22nd of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I've already told you that I did know what happened on the 22nd of January, 1994. It was publicised because children were the victims. That's how I found out. I didn't know about the 8th of August. I knew about the other incident and that's why we are discussing it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, just in order to avoid whatever misunderstanding, we are not discussing events. We are exploring your personal knowledge about these events, just for you to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you accept that you have no personal direct knowledge of this event. What you are able to do is tell us what you read in the media, what you may have heard from other sources, but you yourself do not have any personal, direct knowledge about what happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No, I don't have any direct knowledge nor could I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Witness, one other question. You tell us now that this new element in your statement which reads that it was fired from the Sigma building, that it's an assumption, nothing more, nothing less. Did you tell the Defence that it was an assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But they wrote it down not as an assumption but as a statement of fact and you signed it. Could you explain why you sign a statement stating that it was fired from the Sigma building, where you had told those interviewing you that it was your assumption that this had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I stand by my opinion that it was fired from the Sigma position, but I cannot be absolutely sure because I'm neither an expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in your statement it does not appear as an opinion but it appears as a statement of fact. And to be quite honest, opinions are not what we are seeking primarily from witnesses. We are seeking from witnesses their knowledge based on their personal experience. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I at this point put a question to the witness. Where have you been on the 22nd of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I can't say. It was 22 years ago. It would be abnormal if I remembered that moment. I was somewhere around, probably going about some task I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to switch now to the other incident that is contained in your statement in this case at paragraph 30. It's captioned incident F9. To discuss this case -- this particular incident with you, could I ask that P3 be brought to our screens. It's the Sarajevo map book. And could we go immediately to e-court page 20, a photograph of the neighbourhood where this took place. Now, when you can see the photograph before you, I want you to take your time and make sure you orient yourself. And when you feel you know what's depicted, maybe let me know and then I'll ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Groome, you are recorded as dealing with F9 at paragraph 30 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, that's F9 -- that was paragraph 30 in the Karadzic statement and it is in this particular case it's paragraph 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise for that confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. It's now on our screens so let me know when you've had a chance to study it and then when you have tell me: Do you recognise the neighbourhood that's depicted here?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: This is a part of town called Vojnicko Polje, soldiers field, and Alipasino Polje, and what is marked here is the separation line. So these were the positions controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you now some very specific questions and we'll go one by one so there's no confusion. The high-rise apartment buildings that we see in the background at the top of the picture, that's Alipasino Polje; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is Alipasino Polje and Vojnicko Polje is a bit further below.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can draw your attention to the middle bottom of the photograph, we can see a compound of several buildings that has a red line around it. And my question to you is: Today at transcript page 23 you refer to a location called the Institute for Blind Children and line of separation. Am I correct that's what's contained in that box marked 1 is this area that you've referred to as the Institute for Blind Children?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you refer to another building that -- another facility that catered to blind adults. Can you see that building on this diagram or on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: This is a more recent picture. It was made later. I cannot quite see it on the photograph, but I know the exact juxtaposition. I remember what it looked like before this photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you would be unable to identify it on this photograph although it may be here; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, would you be able to mark the confrontation line on this photograph? And please don't do anything till I give you a specific instruction. Is that something you would be able to do?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So can I ask what colour we're in? Red.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you have a red pen now. Can I ask you to trace the confrontation line as it passes through the area depicted by this photo.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Maybe I got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to delete what you marked, please ask the assistance of the usher and you could start again.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I see that you've drawn a red line right in front of the compound marked as number 1. Where does the confrontation line go from there? You've kind of stopped.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Which way does it go? Where does it go from there on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And now you've drawn another red line that's going down the side of that compound marked number 1; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender P3 -- the version of P3, e-court page 20, that's now been marked by Mr. Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Page 20 of Exhibit P3 as marked by the witness receives number P6512, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6512 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now ask that we go to e-court page 22 of P3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sladoje, this is a photograph taken from this compound that's marked number 1 in this photo. Just give us a moment to bring that to your screen. So again, this is a picture taken from the building marked as number 1, and the red circle in front of you shows you the location where Sanela was shot. My question to you is: Isn't it a fact that at this distance with this line of sight it would be possible to distinguish between a fully grown soldier in uniform and a 16-year-old girl in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I don't know this photograph, but you are right in saying that a soldier can distinguish between a grown soldier and a girl. But this photograph does not mean anything to me. I can't identify anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you also agree that a soldier trained with an ordinary rifle would be able -- at this close distance would have a reasonable possibility of hitting his target?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: He could.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So an optical scope would not be required for firing at a target this distance; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't agree about only one thing. I can't agree that there was a sniper's nest here. I say with full responsibility that there was never a sniper's nest here, and you say there is only one incident scheduled in the indictment relating to this place. It's impossible that there was only one incident if there had been a sniper's nest through four years of the war. My question is: What was the girl doing at the separation line? I suppose that the incident never happened or perhaps it was a stray bullet that hit the girl.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So what is your evidence then, that the incident never happened or you believe a stray bullet hit the girl?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I maintain that there was never a sniper's nest at the school for blind children. I don't know about this incident. I can't say whether it happened or not, but I know that there was never an order given to shoot at civilians. And in the four years of the war there was never an incident directly in the vicinity of the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, will you concede that during the conflict there were soldiers that used that school for blind children? Let's forget about snipers for the moment. Were soldiers -- did soldiers ever occupy and use that facility?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: What do you mean "used"? During the war or before the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the war were soldiers in your battalion ever present in that school for blind children?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, and I said in my statement that there was a position there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've just said: "I don't know about this incident ..." So am I correct in understanding that, just as with the shelling we've talked about, you have no personal or direct knowledge about this girl being shot at this location?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to move to a different topic now. In your statement, D453, in paragraph 14 you say the following: "There was not a single neighbourhood without an enemy unit or military target in it." I want to ask you several questions about this statement. First, when you say there was not a single neighbourhood without a military target in it, are you referring to neighbourhoods in your area of responsibility or are you talking about the entire city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: We can talk about the whole city of Sarajevo because all the features that could be used were used by the military and they turned them into military installations and they mixed with those civilians and that's why collateral damage occurred in incidents involving exchange of fire. I know what you mean. You are trying to say that we claim every part of the city was used for military purposes, but the greatest part of the city was used for military purposes and troops were mixed with civilians. In my own neighbourhood, civilians were mixed in with soldiers and they were collateral damage in every exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to read something you said to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could I seek clarification. You said in your own neighbourhood civilians were mixed in with soldiers and they were collateral damage in every exchange of fire. Are you referring to your neighbourhood, the Serb side or the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the part of town where my unit had its area of responsibility. The civilian population lived side by side by my own troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That clarifies your answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to read you something you said before the Karadzic Chamber and ask you whether you still maintain this and I'm reading from transcript page 30574 in those proceedings. You said: "It is not possible for us to fire at military objectives only without jeopardising the civilian population because they were there and very often civilians were used for that kind of thing." My question to you is whether you believed every time your battalion took some action with respect to the city there was a chance of civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I believe that was so but we had to respond to fire because our positions were in jeopardy. Our troops were in danger, so we had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you consider it a significant chance -- that there was a significant chance of civilian casualties when you took action against the city?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: We did not think that way. We didn't think there would be major casualties. We didn't always know what the disposition was and the civilians were supposed to seek shelter during military action. I cannot tell you in those terms. We had to think about other things, how to defend our positions. Of course we were supposed to have civilians in mind and we tried to minimise civilian casualties, but if they were there then they had to suffer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that shelling or sniping into Sarajevo neighbourhoods that was not in response to specific fire coming out of those neighbourhoods was not militarily justifiable?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: We did not take action if our lines were not jeopardised. I said that in my statement. And we received orders from our superior command to act that way. If some renegade shooter did that, I couldn't control it, we couldn't control it. It's impossible to control.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to paragraph 15 of your statement where you say the following: "The permanent order from my battalion was that we could open fire only in response to enemy fire and only at observed firing targets." Is it your evidence that there were never any orders to fire upon built-up civilian areas absent there being targets which you could observe were firing at your positions?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Never. There was not a single order to target civilians. It's absolutely inconceivable, unfathomable. It's outside all civilian and human norms. I don't see any reason why we would open fire if there had been no fire from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you've kind of mixed up my question now. I wasn't talking about an order to specifically target civilians. I'm asking you about what you've said here that the only -- your standing order was that you were only to engage targets in the city if there was observable fire coming out.

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: It didn't always have to be observed, but if there was fire, and we couldn't always see who was shooting from where, but you can assume, you can estimate, and in those cases we received and gave out orders to open fire. And the story about the civilians is a separate story. We never issued or received orders to target civilians. But civilians did suffer in exchanges of fire but that's a different problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that you never received an order to take action against the city -- well, let me ask -- sorry, strike that. Let me ask another question. Did you ever receive an order to take action against the city because of something that was happening elsewhere in Bosnia far away from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we see 65 ter 30636. It's an order signed by Dragomir Milosevic on the 21st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, that's on your screen now. It's an order signed by Dragomir Milosevic on the 21st of July and it's addressed to several subordinate units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, including the Ilidza Brigade, the Sarajevo Infantry Brigade, and the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. My first question to you is whether the stamp and the document itself appears authentic to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the first paragraph talks about some problems the VRS military is experiencing in several locations. The first thing I want to do is ask for your help in helping the Chamber understand where these locations are. Am I correct that the locations of Cardak, Celina, and Hum are places in the vicinity of Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes, Kragujevac, Cardak, and Hum, yes. Celina is on Trebevic. And as for Trnovo, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we see -- I'm sorry, I'll dispense with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you agree that the distance between Trnovo and Ilidza is approximately 28 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The order also talks about Mount Treskavica. Would you agree with me that that's about 45 kilometres from Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The order also talks about events in Gorazde. Would you agree with me that that's approximately 82 kilometres east of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it may seem like an obvious question but I just want to be clear: You had no type of artillery or other weapon that could give any kind of direct support to the locations mentioned in this order, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So now the paragraph continues: [As read] "Our forces on the Trnovo axis who have a lot of problems, (Kragujevac, Cardak, Hum, Celina have fallen). On top of all other difficulties our defence on Mount Treskavica also has a lot of problems. The Turks have probably moved the main focus of attack towards Gorazde. In order to relieve our forces on the Trnovo axis and to link up the forces and deceive the enemy, I hereby order ..." In this order Milosevic is referring to troops well outside Sarajevo that are experiencing problems; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I have to tell you something. It may go beyond some fears. However, do you know what? When it comes to tactics, when an area is at risk, the focus of war activities is moved to another area. That's why General Milosevic issued that order. You have to know that Gorazde was connected via Trnovo and Treskavica and supplies were done through there. So if you wanted to succeed, you had to open a new theatre of war, you have to open fire in another place, hence that order. So that order was not only with a view to getting to Treskavica or if Ilidza or Trnovo or Gorazde were at risk, the commander of that unit issued an order in order to launch an offensive and to relieve pressure on them as a result of the enemy supremacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now that you've seen the order, do you remember this order, do you remember being ordered to do this?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I've not received this order. It was received by the brigade. As a battalion we may have been in receipt of that order but it would have been pointless. We were engaged in defence. We did not have enough troops to protect the positions that we held and that I marked on the maps that you presented to me previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to remind you again of what you've said in paragraph 15. "The permanent order for my battalion was that we could open fire only in response to enemy fire and only at observed firing targets." The first specific order states -- starts: "The brigade command shall independently plan, prepare, and carry out an attack or a show attack against the city of Sarajevo ..." My question for you is: The phrase "the brigade shall independently plan ..." indicates that the attack on Sarajevo that's being ordered by Dragomir Milosevic is not one that was co-ordinated between the brigades surrounding Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour, for a simple reason. In paragraph 15 which my learned friend is reading from, the witness says very clearly: A permanent order for my battalion ... and what he is being shown is an order for the brigade, and the witness answered that he never received such an order from the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He didn't say so, as a matter of fact. I'll remind you what his evidence was, Mr. Stojanovic. He said that it would not have made sense. Mr. Groome asked him: Do you remember this order. He said: I've not received the order was received by the brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. We may have been in receipt of that, therefore it's unclear whether the witness ever received this order. And could I invite you to be short in your objections and not to make objections argumentative. Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if I can return to my question. The phrase: "The brigade command shall independently plan ..." This indicates that the attack on Sarajevo that's being ordered in this document was not one that was co-ordinated between the brigades surrounding Sarajevo; correct? They were doing it independently?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I've tried to explain what this is about. I don't know what else could I say? When I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: -- was talking about the deployment of units and the refocusing of their activities -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We've heard that evidence and we understand it. My question is simply: According to this order, there's no requirement for the different brigades that could engage Sarajevo to co-ordinate. They're all left to independently plan an attack on Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: You're saying that they were allowed to act independently, but I'm telling you that my battalion did not receive this order from the brigade command and we did not act. So what were we to do in that case?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me just ask you from an experienced, career soldier, when you read what Dragomir Milosevic has ordered, am I correct in understanding that the brigades were not to co-ordinate the attack; they were simply to engage -- to commence an attack on the city of Sarajevo for the reasons you've described, for tactical reasons related to areas outside of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm not a professional soldier. My occupation is different. However, I was forced to be what I was in the war. And now as to what the General wrote, it was his right and it was his duty as the unit commander to defend the positions that were held by the Army of Republika Srpska. If your view is somewhat different, there is nothing I can do about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this order isn't an order to defend territory. This is an order to attack the city of Sarajevo; is that not correct? Am I misreading this order?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: It says here that the city of Sarajevo should be attacked, but it was not meant literally, but rather that fire should be opened on the separation lines or that it should be faked in order to refocus the activities. I don't see anything in dispute in this order from the military point of view. I don't know how you see things yourself. I can't be the judge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, doesn't it contradict your evidence in paragraph 15 -- I'm sorry, I thought I heard something. Doesn't this contradict your evidence in paragraph 15, that you could only open fire in response to enemy fire and only at observed firing targets? Doesn't this contradict your evidence on that point?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No, there's no contradiction at all because units were threatened at other front lines, which means that fire was opened somewhere, maybe in Nedzarici or maybe somewhere else. And this means that our units had to react. When fire was not opened first, I never received an order nor did I issue an order either as commander or as deputy commander to that effect. I don't know how many times I have to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to cut this short. What Mr. Groome is putting to you is the following, that on the one hand side you have testified that you would -- you were ordered to fire exclusively if fire was opened at you, and Mr. Groome reads in this order that apparently brigades were ordered to fire even if they were not fired at but because something had happened at a distance. And he's trying to seek your comment on what he considers an inconsistency in what you stated and what is found in this document. Could you briefly in one or two lines say whether you wish to add anything; if so, please do. If not, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that anything should be added to this. I stick by what I said in paragraph 15. This is all I need to say at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll move on but only after we have taken a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I only have about two more questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two more questions. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, just very short. Very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you think we could finish in, well, let's say five to seven minutes then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps it's preferable to move on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you've just said there's no contradiction at all because units were threatened at other front lines, which means that fire was opened somewhere, maybe in Nedzarici or maybe somewhere else. Aren't you agreeing or aren't you saying right now that you considered it proper to open fire in your battalion because of something that may have been happening at another front line perhaps as far away as Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: When we talk about that, I know what your standpoint is; however, as I've already told you, war is not waged only in one territory. The complete territory where war is waged has to be covered. And people have to adjust to the goings-on everywhere, and this is according to all military doctrines. I can't say anything differently. I can't contradict military doctrines that have been in place for thousands of years, so I don't see what may be in dispute here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And just my final question then: Is your understanding of what you've just described about the war in all the areas and its justification for action in Sarajevo, was that a common understanding among the rank and file of soldiers in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: I apologise. Would you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This concept that you have just explained, the justification of action taken in Sarajevo being something that happened --

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- perhaps far away, my question to you is: Was that a common understanding of your colleagues, of your subordinates, of your superiors in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: That's what they had to do, but not within the same context that you have in mind. You are focusing on the attack on Sarajevo. There were attacks from Sarajevo on our position. There was a war going on. Now, there is a discrepancy in the way --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: -- you think and the way I think together with the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This order requires an attack to commence on the city of Sarajevo on the 22nd of July, 1995. What was -- was there any conflict that you were aware of or any operation by Bosnian forces in Sarajevo on that date that you can tell us about now?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, would you allow me to read this and then I will answer? [As read] "The command of the brigade will independently plan, prepare, or carry out the attack or demonstrate an attack on the city of Sarajevo," but there is a difference there. I was talking about a tactical term, faking fire, so this is not an explicit order to attack the city of Sarajevo or demonstrate an attack on Sarajevo. This is exactly what I'm reading here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you're saying that this order is not a real attack on the city; it's simply a show attack. That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: If this is what it says here, that's what it is, either to carry out an attack or fake an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how you fire a shell into a built-up area such as Sarajevo and it not be an attack?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: And who is it who says that it was ever fired? Who says that it was fired in this case? I don't know that it was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. I'll raise it with another witness. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. I suggest that we take a break first. Could you tell us how much time you would need for re-examination, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we'll see whether there will be enough for finalising the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, could I ask that that exhibit be MFI'd, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30636 receives number P6513, Your Honours, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6513 is marked for identification. We take a break after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom and we'll resume at ten minutes to 2.00. Mr. Mladic, no loud speaking in the courtroom, as you are aware of. Mr. Sladoje, that's the way out, not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at ten minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the witness enters the courtroom, I'd like to briefly address Mr. Mladic and the Defence. There should be no standing up. There should be no greeting. There should be nothing when a witness enters the courtroom. There should be no loud speaking and we'll be very strict in this respect at this stage of the proceedings. Similarly, the Defence is invited to instruct the witnesses that they appear here in their role as a witness not as acquaintances of the accused or being loyal to the accused, whatever. So it should be void of any personal element. That's how we expect witnesses to behave and that's how we expect Mr. Mladic to behave and we'll be strict on it. The witness may enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sladoje, there's no need to seek eye contact with the Defence or with the accused. Would you please keep that in mind. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please look at D457 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you remember this photograph that you marked, the building that you marked, the Institute for the Blind?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you after showing you this image, is this: Your battalion at the line that you marked as the confrontation line, did it at any point during the war -- was it at any point during the war exposed to sniper fire from ABiH positions?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer? They were overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, you were overlapping. Mr. Groome --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't recall -- I object to whether it was raised in cross. I don't recall touching upon this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the photograph admitted from the Prosecution, I think that Mr. Groome did deal with the line of confrontation near the Institute for Blind Children. It's not this precise image but it is a topic that Mr. Groome dealt with, and I'm putting this question to the witness because I would like to put another question to him that has to do with this particular image and that question is as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent Mr. Groome dealt with confrontation lines, it was in response to what was raised by the Defence in the examination. If you have another question for the witness, the witness already I think said something about being exposed to fire from the other side, but please put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honour, if you allow me, I would like to look at document D454 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, there was a question put to you about markings, or rather, what was in the circle that you see below the building of the Geodetski Institute. You said that it was the police station. Now, what I would like to ask you is this: According to your best recollection, how far is the police station from the middle of Gete Street?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Not even 100 or 150 metres. I wasn't in that area very often but I did pass by there, so let's say it was between 100 and 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document 65 ter -- this is the last Prosecution document, 30636.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now P6513.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that's the identification number if I can recall that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sladoje, the first thing I want to ask you is this: Are you aware that in April, on the 26th of April, 1995, the B&H army launched an operation to deblock Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think that's a leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly is. Could you rephrase the question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sladoje, could you please look at the second paragraph of the introduction to the -- of the document where it says: "In order to ease the pressure on our forces on the Trnovo axis, link up our forces, and deceive the enemy I order ..." So is the Trnovo axis the area that was defended by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you knew about the disposition of units of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and the 1st and 4th Corps of the B&H army, would a breakthrough of the ABiH army along the Trnovo axis lead to your brigade being surrounded?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If the forces were to be linked up from the Trnovo axis, the ABiH army units, would your battalion in that case find itself completely encircled by all the positions in relation to positions of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: It was already encircled but had this happened, then it would be encircled even more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just that these are leading questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they are. And apart from that, they are beyond the point raised in cross-examination. In cross-examination the issue was raised whether the statement of the witness saying that they would fire only in response of fire directed against themselves, whether that was consistent with what is in this document. Now you move far away from all that, Mr. Stojanovic, and you do it by putting leading questions to the witness. Well, the witness has answered the question, let's move on and let's try to avoid this to happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour, and I am trying not to put leading questions here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to put one more question to you relating to paragraph 15 of your statement to the Defence. Are you able to tell us if in July 1995 you had any type of order from the brigade command which would deviate from orders up until that time about the manner that fire should be utilised?

utterances.speaker: MILE SLADOJE
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sladoje, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Groome, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This then concludes your testimony, Mr. Sladoje. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No greeting. Instruction should be clear for the next witnesses. I'm looking at the clock. I don't know whether it makes much sense to start the examination of the next witness. Perhaps it's better to adjourn for the day. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then unless there would be anything any of the parties would like to raise, we'll adjourn for the day and we resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 20th of May, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of May, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.04 p.m.,
